hints: Focus on what the cations can actually do chemically, not just their size or charge. One of them can behave as an acid.
Remember that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is a sparingly soluble base, so think about what would happen if $\text{OH}^-$ ions were removed from solution.
Connect $\text{NH}_4^+$ reacting with $\text{OH}^-$ to form $\text{NH}_3$ and water, and see how this pulls the dissolving equilibrium to the right in a way $\text{Na}^+$ cannot.
walkthrough:
**Why Mg(OH)2 is normally insoluble**

Think of magnesium hydroxide as sitting in a delicate equilibrium. Only a tiny amount dissolves.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$$

**Compare Na+ and NH4+**

$\text{Na}^+$ is from a strong base, so it is neutral and does nothing to water or to $\text{OH}^-$. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of a weak base ($\text{NH}_3$), so it can donate a proton.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq)$$

**See how NH4+ removes OH- and dissolves the solid**

The $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{NH}_4^+$ neutralises the $\text{OH}^-$ from the $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$. By Le Chatelier's principle, removing $\text{OH}^-$ pulls the first equilibrium to the right, so more solid dissolves. $\text{NaCl}$ cannot do this.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

options.A: Ionic radius similarity does not control solubility here. Dissolving involves an acid-base reaction, not fitting ions into a lattice. This is a distractor using size as if it were the key factor.
options.B: Both $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NaCl}$ are soluble ionic salts and dissociate essentially fully in water. Degree of dissociation is not the difference, and even if it were, less dissociation would not explain greater dissolving power.
options.C: It is true that $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ are both isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons), but this fact has no effect on the solubility equilibrium of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$. It is an irrelevant true statement.
options.D: This is correct and reassuring. $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as a Brønsted-Lowry acid and donates a proton to $\text{OH}^-$, forming $\text{NH}_3$ and water. This removes $\text{OH}^-$ and drives $\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$ to the right, so the solid dissolves.
